activity: to compute the electric field strength at a point between two charged plates
knowledge_domain: to compute the electric field strength at a point between two charged plates
fact: Two parallel plates 0.02 metres apart with 100 volts across them produce an electric field of 5,000 volts per metre between them.
story:
The physics lab smelled of warm dust and the lemon cleaner the janitor used on the benches, and Christopher had commandeer of the back table by arriving at 7:40, twenty minutes before anyone else. Two brass plates stood clipped to a frame, a ruler beside them, and a yellow index card on which Ms. Van Dijk had written, in her narrow hand, the only instructions she ever gave for this exercise: 100 volts across the plates; find the field strength between them. He measured the gap twice, once from the inside faces and once from the clips, because he could not decide which she meant, and wrote 2 cm in his notebook. He was still holding the ruler when the door opened and Sophie came in with her bag over one shoulder and a folded piece of paper she did not seem to know she was carrying.

"You're here early," she said. "That's ominous."

"Retake on Friday," Christopher said. "The one I got a fifty-two on." He did not tell her the other half of it, that his father had looked at the fifty-two and then looked at him in a way that was worse than shouting, and had said only, "Physics is physics. It doesn't move. You're the one who moved." He turned the notebook so she couldn't see the margin where he had written and crossed out the same sentence three times.

Sophie sat down across from him and finally noticed the paper in her hand. "This got put in my locker. Wrong locker, I think. It's got your name on it." She slid it over. The handwriting was Izaiah's, unmistakable because Izaiah pressed so hard the words showed through the page: "Check the answer I sent you last night. The one you said was too big. I redid it. Trust me this time."

Christopher remembered the message from last night, remembered lying on his bed with the phone above his face and the arboreal shadow of the maple outside his window moving across the ceiling. Izaiah had texted a worked solution at 11:20: field equals voltage over distance, 100 over 2, answer 50 volts per metre. Christopher had replied that 50 sounded small for something that could pull sparks, and Izaiah had answered, "It's plates, not lightning," and then gone offline. He had fallen asleep with the problem unresolved, which was its own kind of unrest.

He looked at the plates now. "He divided 100 by 2," he said slowly. "The gap's 2 centimetres."

"So?"

"So that's the problem." He took the ruler up again, then put it down and picked up his pencil instead, the way Ms. Van Dijk had shown them the first week, back in September, when the whole class had stood at these same benches and she had said only, "Measure like the formula expects," and refused to say more while Izaiah groaned and someone knocked over a stand. Christopher hadn't understood her then. He thought he might be starting to. The formula wanted the gap in metres, and the gap was 0.02 metres, and 100 divided by 0.02 was not 50. He did it on paper, then again in the margin, then a third time in a different corner of the page because he did not trust the first two.

"Five thousand," he said. "Volts per metre. Izaiah's answer is a hundred times too small." He said it quietly, because the door had opened again and Izaiah himself had come in, hood up, earbuds trailing, moving toward them with the unhurried confidence of someone who believes he has already finished.

"Chris," Izaiah said, pulling out the chair between them, "did you get my note? I checked it four ways. Fifty. Ms. Van Dijk grades off the answer, you know that." He set his own notebook down, open to a page dense with confident arithmetic, and tapped it.

Christopher looked at Izaiah's page and then at his own. He understood the shape of the choice: agree, and be wrong together, which was safer; or say what he'd found and watch Izaiah's face do the thing it did when he was contradicted. He thought about the fifty-two, about his father, about Ms. Van Dijk leaning against the bench in September with her arms folded, letting them flounder on purpose. Maybe the floundering had been the lesson. Maybe there was no lesson and she just liked watching them figure it out. Both of those felt true and he couldn't make them into one.

"You measured in centimetres," Christopher said. "Two centimetres. But it's 0.02 metres. You have to divide 100 by 0.02." He turned his notebook around and slid it across the bench, the way Sophie had slid the note to him, one uncertain thing passed hand to hand all morning.

Izaiah looked at the page for a long moment. Outside, the first bell hadn't rung yet; the room held only the hum of the overhead lights and, faintly, a lawnmower somewhere on the far field. His pencil hovered over his own numbers, not crossing anything out, not writing anything new. Sophie leaned in to see.

"Five thousand," Izaiah said at last, and this time it wasn't a claim, it was a question, and before Christopher could answer, the door at the front of the room opened and Ms. Van Dijk came in carrying the stack of Friday's retakes.

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: The 2026 FIFA World Cup, hosted by Canada, Mexico and the United States, was the first with 48 teams and the first hosted by three countries.
story:
The stadium smelled like cut grass and frying onions, and Chloe had been acclimating to the noise for an hour without quite managing it. Her father had bought the tickets in March, when the draw put the match in their city, and he kept touching the brim of his cap as though confirming it was still there. On her left sat Bianca, who had worn face paint and then wiped most of it off in the car; on her right, Madison, who was reading the program with the concentration of someone studying for an exam.

"Forty-eight teams," Madison said. "I'm telling you, this time it's forty-eight. My cousin kept arguing with me at dinner. He said thirty-two, like always."

"He's wrong," Bianca said. "It's more than that. It's the first one with forty-eight."

Chloe said nothing, because she had spent the drive telling them both, with more certainty than she felt, that the number didn't change anything that mattered. More teams meant more matches meant more money, and the whole thing was a machine. She had a whole speech about it. Now the teams were walking out onto the grass and her speech felt like something she'd rehearsed in a mirror.

"You're quiet," Madison said.

"I'm thinking about my cousin."

"You don't have a cousin."

The crowd rose for the anthem and saved her from answering. Somewhere behind them a man was singing so loudly and so badly that Bianca's shoulders started shaking, and Chloe's father joined in on the second verse, soft and off-key, and Chloe found she was singing too.

Three summers ago, before her mother left, they had watched a match on the couch with the sound low because her mother had a headache. Her mother knew nothing about the sport and kept asking why the goalkeeper was allowed to use his hands and nobody else was, and Chloe, who was thirteen and impatient, had explained it in a tone she regretted for months afterward. Her mother had said, "I like asking you things," and Chloe had understood, even at thirteen, that this was a compliment she hadn't earned and would have to earn later.

In the twelfth minute a midfielder she'd never heard of hit a shot from thirty meters that struck the crossbar so hard the sound reached them like something seismic, a low thump in the chest, and eighty thousand people made a noise that was not quite a groan and not quite a cheer. Bianca grabbed Chloe's arm. Madison dropped the program. Her father stood up with his hands on his head.

"Did you see that," Bianca said, not a question.

"It hit the bar," Chloe said. "It was this close."

Her father leaned over during the restart. "Three countries, you know," he said. "First time it's been three. Canada, Mexico, us."

"Thirty-two," Madison muttered. "My cousin is going to be insufferable either way."

Chloe had been thinking about her father's peccadilloes during the drive, the way he narrated the route, the way he claimed to have predicted every goal ever scored, and she had filed the trip under the heading of things she was tolerating. But the shot off the crossbar had rearranged something. She thought about the couch, the low sound, her mother's questions. The tournament was a machine and also it was this: a man she didn't know hitting a bar from thirty meters and a whole stadium feeling it in the sternum at once.

The goal came in the sixty-first minute, a scrappy thing off a corner, deflected twice, and Chloe was on her feet before she decided to stand. Bianca was screaming. Madison was holding the program over her head like a flag. Her father had both arms around strangers.

"It's forty-eight," Chloe shouted at Madison over the noise. "You were right. Tell your cousin. First time with forty-eight, and the first time three countries hosted it. Canada, Mexico, the United States."

Madison's face did something complicated. "You said the number didn't matter."

"I was wrong about that. I think. Some of it matters."

"Some of it," Madison repeated, grinning, and wrote something on the back of the program, presumably ammunition for her cousin.

The match ended one to nothing, and the crowd filed out through the gates into a night that smelled like rain coming. Bianca's face paint had sweated into faint blue streaks. Her father talked about the goal the entire walk to the car, and Chloe let him narrate, and even asked him a question about the offside rule she already knew the answer to, just to hear him explain it.

At the car, Madison tore the corner off the program and handed it over. On it she'd written, in her terrible handwriting, "48 teams, 3 countries, FIRST," and beneath that, "Chloe was wrong, written down so she can't deny it."

"I'm not denying it," Chloe said, folding the paper into her pocket anyway. "I'm keeping the evidence."

Her father unlocked the doors and the interior light came on, and inside the car it was warm and quiet and hers.

activity: to explain how DNA is copied and turned into protein through transcription and translation
knowledge_domain: to explain how DNA is copied and turned into protein through transcription and translation
fact: Translation usually begins at the codon AUG, which also codes for the amino acid methionine.
story:
The Saturday shift at the Fairhaven Veterinary Clinic began with a tomcat named Bruce attempting to eviscerate the third chair from the window, and Jade pinning him gently against her chest while the technician drew blood. Between appointments she kept her flashcards on the reception counter, face down, because Dr. Patel had asked her twice not to "study molecule things" where clients could see them. She was supposed to be learning transcription and translation for the science fair on Monday, and so far she had learned only that the cell did everything in an order she kept getting wrong.

Alyson was supposed to be learning it with her. They had divided the work in September, when the project still seemed like something they would do together at Alyson's kitchen table, and by November Alyson had stopped answering texts about it. The exhibit board, half built, sat in Jade's garage with Alyson's handwriting on exactly one panel. Jade had decided, that morning, to finish it alone, and to stop pretending that hurt less than it did.

At eleven, a woman brought in a border collie with a padlocked plastic cone around its neck, having somehow locked it herself with her teeth, and while Jade filled out the form the door chime went again. Mr. Silva-Jayasuriya came in with his old spaniel, Nina, shuffling on her bad hip, and behind him came Alyson, holding a shoebox of paper strips like an offering.

"You work here," Alyson said. It wasn't a question.

"I work here."

Mr. Silva-Jayasuriya lowered himself into the chair Bruce had spared and watched the two of them with open interest, the way he watched everything. He was their old biology teacher, retired in June, and he lived three doors down from Alyson; Jade had never known that until this moment. "I'll mind Nina," he said. "You two go sort whatever that is."

They took the shoebox into the back room where the samples were logged, and Alyson set it on the counter beside Jade's flashcards. "I came to give these back," Alyson said. "The strips. For the board. I cut them all."

"You cut them."

"Three weeks ago. I was going to text you." She didn't say why she hadn't. In the silence, Jade could hear the dryer spinning in the kennel room, could smell the antiseptic and underneath it the warm animal smell that never came out of anything.

Alyson had come, at least, in part, for a truce, though neither of them would have used that word. She stood at the counter while Jade unpacked the strips, and Jade, instead of accepting the peace, pulled out the mRNA puzzle they'd been assigned for the fair's interactive table: a long paper ribbon of letters, U's and C's and G's and A's, that visitors were supposed to decode into amino acids using the chart. Jade had been practicing all week, and every time, the answer came out as gibberish, amino acids that spelled nothing a protein would ever be.

She laid the ribbon out now, under the fluorescent light, and decoded the first three letters again. "G, G, U," she said. "Glycine. Then U, A, A. Stop." She flattened the ribbon with both palms. "It stops almost immediately. The whole thing is garbage after that. I've done it fifteen times."

Alyson picked up the other end of the ribbon, the end Jade always ignored because it was just the loose trailing edge, and read it through once, slowly. Jade watched her lips move. "It's not garbage," Alyson said finally. "You're starting in the wrong place."

In the other room, Mr. Silva-Jayasuriya's voice carried faintly through the door, telling the technician about a rock garden he was building, about how the black stone was igneous, born from volcanoes, and how he liked owning something older than every dog he'd ever lost. Jade held the ribbon and turned Alyson's sentence over. Wrong place. Not wrong letters, not a broken chart. She had assumed the string began where the printing began.

She walked her fingers along the letters from Alyson's end until she found the sequence A, U, G, and stopped. "Start here?"

"Try it."

Jade ran her finger along the codons from that point, and the chart gave her a protein, an actual sensible chain, amino acid after amino acid with no premature stops. She wrote the first one on the counter pad and stared at it. "Methionine," she said. "The first one is always methionine. Translation usually begins at the codon AUG, and AUG codes for methionine." She said it out loud and it sounded less like a fact from her flashcards and more like something she had found on the floor and turned over.

"The start codon," Alyson said. "It's called the start codon."

The twist, when it came, was small and quiet. Jade flipped the ribbon over and found, in Alyson's handwriting, faint pencil marks bracketing the AUG, and beside them a note dated in October. Alyson had decoded this puzzle weeks ago, alone, at her kitchen table, the night after she'd stopped answering texts. "You already solved it," Jade said.

"I was going to bring it over. Then I didn't. Then it got weird, and then it got too late to make it not weird." Alyson straightened the strips in the shoebox so their edges lined up. "You did it yourself just now anyway. I just pointed."

Jade wanted to say that pointing was the whole of it, that starting was the whole of it, but she also remembered every unanswered text and knew the rapprochement was not finished, only begun. She rolled up the ribbon and held it out, and Alyson took it.

At the window, Mr. Silva-Jayasuriya was signing Nina's file, and the woman with the border collie had given up on the cone entirely and was letting the dog wear it like a crown. Jade pulled her flashcards off the counter, squared them, and offered the whole stack, not just the ribbon.

"Monday, then," Alyson said.

"Monday," Jade said, and pocketed the counter pad with methionine still written on it.

activity: the idea that present decisions can connect to consequences years in the future
knowledge_domain: the idea that present decisions can connect to consequences years in the future
fact: The Framingham Heart Study, which began following residents of Framingham, Massachusetts in 1948, gave medicine the term 'risk factor' for habits and conditions that raise later disease risk.
story:
The envelope arrived on a Tuesday, cream-colored and official, addressed to her grandfather with the return address of a clinic Madeline had never heard of. She set it on the kitchen table beside his coffee cup and tried not to stare at it while he read the newspaper, but the seal had already been broken, which meant he had read it that morning and said nothing, and the silence felt like a held breath.

"Grandpa, what's the letter?"

"Questionnaire." He turned a page. "They want to know what I eat, how I sleep, whether I smoke."

"You don't smoke," Madeline said, and watched his hand, which had gone very still on the newspaper. That was the moment the room changed, though she could not have said how. Something in the way he didn't answer.

She had found the butts two weeks ago, behind the garage in a coffee tin she'd thought was full of screws. She had carried the knowledge around since then like a stone in her pocket, turning it over, deciding against telling her mother, then deciding for it, then not deciding at all. Telling felt like betrayal. Not telling felt like one too, just a slower kind, the kind you could live with for years before it presented its bill. She didn't have a word for that yet, but her grandfather did.

"Whole town in Massachusetts," he said that evening, peeling an apple in one long ribbon while she pretended to do homework. "Framingham. Doctors started following everybody there in 1948. Followed them for decades. That's why my doctor asks about habits now instead of just treating you when you drop."

"Following them how?"

"Watched what they did, year after year, and waited to see who got sick." He let the peel fall into the sink. "Gave medicine a whole new term for it. Risk factor. That's what they call a habit or a condition that raises your chance of disease later on."

"So a cigarette now is a heart attack in 1985." Madeline said it lightly, the way you say a thing so it lands soft.

"Something like that." He looked at her over the apple. "You accusing me of arithmetic?"

"I'm saying the tin behind the garage isn't full of screws."

The peel went into the compost and he washed his hands for longer than hands needed washing. Madeline heard her mother's voice from earlier that week, the way she'd denigrate his stubbornness at dinner, calling him a man who wouldn't change for anyone, and Madeline had sat there silent, protecting him with her silence, and it struck her that everyone in the house was managing everyone else with what they declined to say. On the phone that night, Jolie argued she had to tell her mom immediately, that keeping it secret wasn't tenable, not with a questionnaire from a cardiology clinic sitting on the table. Keira took the other side: it was his body, his business, his doctor, his choice. Madeline lay in the dark holding both positions like two stones of equal weight, unable to set either down.

In the morning she found him at the kitchen table with the questionnaire and a pen, reading glasses low on his nose, and she saw that the answer spaces were filled in, all of them, in his careful draftsman's hand. He had written the word yes. He had written it more than once. He looked up and caught her looking.

"Took me a week," he said. "Forty years I told doctors no. Figured the lie was cheaper than the lecture." He tapped the page. "Turns out the study people had it right about that too. Everything you do now is a letter to who you'll be in thirty years. I just decided to stop forging the signature."

Madeline sat down across from him, the accusation she'd rehearsed all night dissolving into something smaller and stranger. She had wanted to change his mind, and instead he had changed it himself, before she ever got the chance, and she felt both relieved and cheated of her whole moral drama. Then he slid a second envelope across the table, the one addressed to her, from her school, a health form requiring a parent's signature.

"Yours came yesterday," he said. "I noticed you left the energy drink part blank."

"I noticed you put the coffee tin back with fresh screws."

He laughed, one short bark, and sealed his envelope with a flat of his hand. "Mail mine first," he said, holding it out to her. "And fill yours out honest. I'll drive you to the box."

activity: to solve projectile motion problems by separating horizontal and vertical velocity components
knowledge_domain: to solve projectile motion problems by separating horizontal and vertical velocity components
fact: Near Earth's surface a projectile's vertical velocity changes by about 9.8 metres per second every second, whether it is rising or falling.
story:
The garage belonged to Mr. Nolan, who had left it to Sarah every Tuesday evening on the understanding that she would not subjugate his workbench to her physics homework, a word he used with evident satisfaction. She spread her notebook on an upturned milk crate instead, beside a coffee tin of screws she was under orders not to disturb, and read the problem again. A ball launched at fourteen metres per second at thirty degrees above the horizontal. How far does it travel before landing. The horizontal part she could do. It was the vertical part that had begun, over the course of three evenings, to feel like a personal insult.

Kellen came through the side door carrying an amp, because Tuesdays were also, in Kellen's account, band nights, an arrangement that had never actually been agreed to by anyone. "You're not seriously doing math in a garage," Kellen said, setting the amp down on the far side, which was at least a gesture toward diplomacy. "This is a space for art." He had a demo to record by Friday for a guy his cousin knew at a venue downtown, and the garage, he claimed, had the right reverb. Sarah did not ask how a concrete floor could have reverb. She said he could have it after she threw the ball.

She had brought a tennis ball and her phone, and a plan she'd worked out on the bus: throw the ball straight up, time it, compare the numbers. Kellen held the phone, truculent about being a stopwatch rather than an audience, and counted down anyway as though the ball were a headliner. Sarah threw. The ball rose past the shelf of paint cans, hung for an instant near the fluorescent tube, and came down into her hands. Kellen called out the time. She did it again, and again, marking each trial in the notebook, and after the fourth throw she stopped, because the numbers were wrong in a way she could not immediately name.

She had expected the descent to be quicker. It looked quicker, the way a dropped thing always looks more urgent than a rising thing, and she had assumed the ball lost speed coming up faster than it gained it going down. But her timings said the two halves of the flight matched. She worked it on paper, turning the total time into a rate of change, and there it was: the vertical speed was changing by about 9.8 metres per second every second on the way up, and by the same 9.8 every second on the way down. She said it out loud to check it against her own ears. "It slows up and speeds down at the exact same rate. Whether it's rising or falling, nine point eight every second." Kellen, who had been coiling a cable, said, "Cool," in the tone of a man being told about a horseshoe crab.

What it meant, she saw with the particular pleasure of two separate ideas agreeing, was that she could stop treating the ball's flight as one stubborn tangle. The vertical motion had its own arithmetic, uniform and indifferent, while the horizontal speed just carried on the whole time, unbothered, like a second passenger on the same train who never looks out the window. She split the fourteen metres per second into a vertical part and a horizontal part, gave the vertical part over to the 9.8, and let the horizontal part multiply by time in peace. The answer came out in four lines instead of the page of flailing she'd produced on Sunday.

Her phone buzzed with a message from Tyra, who was at her cousin's watching a documentary and had opinions. "Did you know some moths in industrial cities got darker because the pollution darkened the trees, so the dark phenotype blended in and survived better. Anyway. Are you getting the projectile stuff or do we both fail Friday. My mother has already told three people I'm going into engineering. I would like a say in this." Sarah typed back that she was getting it, mostly, and that Tyra's mother did not get a vote on the phenotype of anyone's future. Then she sat with the word mostly, because it was the true one. She understood the splitting. She did not understand why the upward and downward rates matched so neatly, only that they did, and she wrote that distinction in the margin, unsure whether it counted as honesty or as a hole in her knowledge shaped exactly like a virtue.

Kellen had plugged in the amp and was tuning to something he described as a minor key with a secret. "So the ball thing," he said over the hum. "If you throw it up at like nine point eight metres per second, does it just, stop being a number?" Sarah considered this, decided it was not the stupidest question she'd heard this week, and said she'd find out, which she suspected was the whole trade she was signing up for.

She threw the ball straight up one more time, harder, so it nearly kissed the ceiling, and counted the seconds under her breath until it filled her hands again.

activity: going on a first date
knowledge_domain: going on a first date
fact: Psychologists call it misattribution of arousal when a racing heart caused by fear or excitement is mistaken for attraction to the person nearby.
story:
The rink smelled of cold rubber and burnt sugar from the snack bar, and Alice stood at the boards with her skates laced wrong on purpose, too loose, so she would have an excuse to sit down again. Her date's name was printed on the rental sticker, THEO, half peeled already. He had told her on the walk over that he was something of a raconteur, and then told a story about a seagull stealing his sandwich that was, in fairness, pretty funny, though the word raconteur had sat strangely in her mouth all evening, like a pebble under the tongue.

They had met in the line for the Ferris wheel at Lara's birthday fair, where the ride had jammed with the two of them suspended at the top for twenty minutes and he had talked the whole time, cheerful and unbothered, while Alice's hands went white on the bar. It was possible she liked him. It was also possible she had just been very high up.

Now he wobbled out onto the ice and fell almost immediately, laughing, and she skated a slow circle around him while he got up. He fell twice more on the far turn, and the second time a refraction of ice spray caught the overhead lights, and Alice noticed her own heart going hard against her ribs, quick and unaccountable, the way it had gone at the top of the wheel. She slowed. There was nothing to be afraid of here. The ice was resurfaced, the crowd sparse and gentle, the worst outcome a bruise.

She thought of Eve, who wanted to study psychology and said so at every available opening. Last spring, before exams, Eve had been reading with her feet on the radiator, and she had looked up and said, "Did you know there's a thing called misattribution of arousal? A racing heart from fear or excitement gets mistaken for attraction to the person nearby." She had said it in her flat, recitation voice, the one she used for facts she was proud of, and then gone back to her book. Alice had filed it away without examining it, the way you put a coin in a coat pocket and forget the coat.

But tonight the pocket turned itself out. She tested it the way you test a loose tooth. She let herself imagine Theo falling, properly, cracking his wrist, the long ambulance drive, her mother's face at the hospital, and felt the fear bloom and her pulse climb with it, indiscriminate, the same climbing she had felt watching him wave his arms on the ice. Then she imagined him taking her hand at the boards, and the flutter that followed was quieter, harder to locate, less like an alarm and more like the low fizz of something fermenting in a jar in a cupboard, going about its slow work unseen. Were those the same feeling? Was either of them the one people called liking somebody?

"Are you having a moral crisis over there?" Theo called. He had made it forty feet without falling and was visibly pleased about it.

"I'm conducting an experiment," she said, and skated over to tell him about Eve and the study and the word, because it seemed dishonest not to, and because she wanted to watch his face while she said it.

He listened, wobbling, arms out like a tightrope walker. "So you're saying you can't tell if you like me or if you're just scared."

"I'm saying I can't tell yet. Those might not even be different things on the ice."

"That's the most bombastic thing anyone's ever said to me while I'm this bad at skating," he said, and then the ice took his feet out from under him and he went down hard on his tailbone, and Alice was already halfway to him before she thought about it, her heart going like a kettle, and she knelt and asked if he was okay, and he said yes, and then, because the moment was going soft and strange, "So what's the verdict?"

She looked at him, at the wet mark spreading dark across the seat of his jeans, at his hopeful, ridiculous face. "The verdict is I'm going to need more trials," she said, and held out her hand to pull him up.

activity: to explain how greenhouse gases trap heat and read a graph of carbon dioxide over the last century
knowledge_domain: to explain how greenhouse gases trap heat and read a graph of carbon dioxide over the last century
fact: In 1859, John Tyndall began laboratory experiments measuring how gases absorb infrared heat, showing that water vapor and carbon dioxide absorb it while nitrogen and oxygen do not.
story:
The quarry water was green where it was shallow and black where the old machines had dug deepest, and Luca stood on the ledge with Nathan's phone in his hand, scrolling through the draft of his report instead of jumping. Two weeks until the resubmission deadline, and Mr. Ionescu had written one incisive line across the top of the first attempt: "You explain the graph as if it were self-evident. It isn't. Show me where the physics comes from." Luca had written three paragraphs about the Keeling curve, the steady climb of carbon dioxide across the decades, and had called the greenhouse effect "a recent discovery," which was the phrase Mr. Ionescu had circled twice.

"You're supposed to be off the phone," Nathan said. "Whole point of coming out here."

"Give me ten minutes." Luca sat on the warm limestone instead, his heels hanging over the drop. Nathan was already in the water, arms spread, shouting about the cold. Mustafa lowered himself down the goat path with his sandals in his teeth, the careful one, the pragmatist, the boy who tested the depth with a rope and a wrench before he ever jumped.

Luca searched the name Mr. Ionescu had pencilled in the margin, small and tilted, like something he hadn't wanted to make official. Tyndall. The results came up before Luca expected them to. He read, then read again, then looked out at the water where Nathan floated on his back, and felt something rearrange behind his eyes.

"Listen to this," Luca called down. "In 1859, John Tyndall started doing lab experiments. Measuring how gases absorb infrared heat."

Nathan flipped over and blew water off his lips. "Hundred and whatever years before us. So?"

"So carbon dioxide absorbs it. Water vapor absorbs it. And nitrogen and oxygen don't. That's the whole thing. That's the greenhouse effect. It's not modern at all."

Mustafa had reached the bottom of the path and stood wringing out the hem of his shirt, though he hadn't gone in. "Wait. People figured that out before cars?"

"That's what it says. He measured it. In a laboratory." Luca turned the phone so the glare moved off the screen. "I wrote that it was discovered recently. Like, satellites, the seventies, whatever. He circled it."

"So fix the sentence," Nathan said, and dove under, and his body undulated once in the green light and was gone.

But Luca couldn't just fix the sentence, and he knew it while he was still sitting there. He opened the report again and looked at the graph he'd pasted in, carbon dioxide rising year over year, the line's slope steepening as it approached the present. He had treated the line like an accusation, like something that argued for him, and Mr. Ionescu had seen it. The line didn't argue anything. Tyndall had shown what the gases did; the graph showed what had happened to the air; between the two sat everything Luca actually believed, and he had put none of it down.

Mustafa climbed up beside him and looked at the screen. "You're going to sit here the whole time."

"I'm figuring something out." Luca set the phone face-down on the rock. "Here's my problem. Nathan thinks because it was measured in 1859, it's settled, done, boring. And I used to think the graph settled it too. But it doesn't. The graph tells you what changed. Tyndall tells you what the gases can do. Neither one tells you what I think, or what anyone should do about it. That part's still mine to say."

Mustafa picked up a shard of limestone and weighed it in his palm. "So say it. Or say you don't know. Both are allowed, I think."

"I don't know some of it. I know that much." Luca stood, and the drop looked different from standing, longer and more serious. "I'm going to rewrite it from the experiment forward. 1859, what he measured, which gases, which didn't absorb. Then the graph as the consequence. Then a paragraph where I actually say what I think and where I stop being sure."

"That's the whole structure of the thing," Mustafa said. "You just did the report out loud, sitting on a cliff in your boxers."

Luca laughed, and something in his chest unlocked, the same feeling as the moment before a jump when the decision has already been made and the body is only catching up. He put the phone in his shoe, laced it to his wrist, and walked to the edge. Below, Nathan surfaced and shouted his name, and Mustafa was already measuring the drop with his eyes, calculating, calculating, and Luca stepped off into the cold green dark with his arms out.

activity: terms related to responsibility, trade-offs and unintended consequences used in structured ethical reasoning
knowledge_domain: terms related to responsibility, trade-offs and unintended consequences used in structured ethical reasoning
fact: A Pareto improvement, named after economist Vilfredo Pareto, is a change that makes at least one person better off without making anyone worse off.
story:
The fourth-floor vending machine ate Matthew's dollar on the first Saturday of November, and by the second Saturday he had learned to feed it the way you'd feed a nervous animal, slowly, one bill at a time. That was the kind of knowledge nobody put on a college application, and yet the application was the reason he was here at all, in blue polyester, pushing a cart of magazines toward the east wing where the light went thin and crepuscular by four in the afternoon. Two hours a week, a signature from the volunteer coordinator, a line that said he was the kind of person who did this. He was still deciding whether he was.

In room 410 a man named Mr. Jean-Louis sat with a blanket over his knees and a paperback open to a page he did not appear to be reading. He had been a history teacher, he told Matthew the first time he came in, for thirty-one years, and he still corrected people who said things like "back then" without specifying when. "Back then is a lazy phrase," he said. "Every moment is somebody's back then." Matthew liked him without being able to say exactly why, the way he liked certain songs before he knew the words.

The trouble began at the nurses' station, where Jana was waiting for him with her arms crossed. She wanted his gift shop slot, the one facing the elevator bank, and she wanted it starting immediately. Rami, who stocked the shop on Sundays and had opinions about everything, had told her Matthew would trade, because Matthew always traded. "You gave Dev your parking spot at homecoming," she said. "You gave me your lab goggles for a week." She was not wrong. He had built a small reputation on being easy, and he was only now noticing what it had cost him, which was the ability to say no without rehearsing it.

"I'll think about it," he said, and she rolled her eyes in a way that suggested she had heard that before, from him, about something.

Rami found him in the supply closet where the good pillows were hidden. "You know what my econ teacher calls a fair trade?" Rami said, pulling a crate of juice cups toward him. "A Pareto improvement, named after an economist called Vilfredo Pareto. It's a change that makes at least one person better off without making anyone worse off. Both sides gain, nobody loses." He said it the way he said most things, like a fact he was holding out for inspection, half-proud and half-skeptical.

"So if I give Jana the shop," Matthew said slowly, working it out with his hands still full of pillows, "and I get nothing back, that's not a Pareto improvement. That's just me being worse off." Rami shrugged. "Unless you count whatever you get out of being a pushover." It was meant as a joke. It landed somewhere else.

He remembered then, a memory arriving the way smells do, unannounced. Two years ago, before his grandfather went into a home, Matthew had driven him to appointments in his mother's car, and his grandfather had always wanted the radio on, and Matthew had always wanted it off, and one afternoon they had compromised by finding a station neither of them hated. His grandfather had called it the diplomatic channel and laughed until he coughed. It had felt, at the time, like the smallest thing in the world. Matthew had not thought about it in a year, and it came back to him now with a weight he did not expect, the smell of the old car's vinyl, the sun on the dashboard, the sound of someone laughing who did not laugh often.

He carried the magazines into 410 anyway, because the schedule said 410, and because Mr. Jean-Louis had requested something about the Boer War and Matthew had actually found one in the donation box. Mr. Jean-Louis took the book, looked over Matthew's shoulder at the door, and said, "That girl who sits at the station. The one with the braid. She's been reading the same page of a visitors log for forty minutes." He turned the paperback in his hands. "In thirty-one years of teaching, I learned that when a student stares at nothing, the something is elsewhere. Room 412 is just down the hall. There's a woman recuperating in there who's been alone all week."

Matthew stood very still. He had walked past 412 twice that morning.

He found Jana at the station, still holding the visitors log, and he did not say I'll think about it. He said, "Your grandmother's in 412, isn't she." It was not a question, and she did not treat it as one. She looked at the elevator doors, then at the floor, and her voice came out smaller than she intended it to. "They only let two visitors at a time and my aunt takes both slots in the morning. Evenings I could get in, but the shop closes at five and the shift ends at six." She pushed the log aside. "I wasn't going to say that part."

"Here's what we'll do," Matthew said. "You take the gift shop. I take your cart rounds, which end on this floor." He was already rewriting the schedule in his head, both shifts, both floors, counting who gained what. Maybe it wasn't clean; maybe somebody, somewhere, was a little worse off, and maybe he was tired of pretending that every good arrangement could be one where no one paid anything. Some trades had a cost, and you paid it on purpose.

At five the corridor lights dimmed themselves and the windows went violet. Matthew pushed the cart down the east wing, and through the open door of room 412 he saw two braids bent close together over a hospital bed, and heard a voice, low and steady, telling some story about a woman who was already laughing at the ending.

"Don't you move that cart," Mr. Jean-Louis called after him from 410. "You left the Boer War in reach, and I intend to be unreasonable about it."

activity: to check a viral video's source and date with a reverse image search before sharing it
knowledge_domain: to check a viral video's source and date with a reverse image search before sharing it
fact: Google added 'search by image' in 2011, letting users upload a picture or paste its link to find where else it appears on the web.
story:
Michael's grandmother had discovered the forward button the way some people discover religion, and by June her emails arrived in waves: a shark on a flooded highway, a soldier carrying a child, a politician supposedly saying something the caption insisted he had said. She lived two floors up, in the same house, so the emails were redundant in a way she never seemed to notice; she would send one at nine and knock on his door at ten to ask if he had seen it.

The photo that Tuesday showed a city street underwater, boats where cars should be, a man on a roof waving a shirt. The caption said it had been taken that morning, in a city Michael had actually heard of, and it ended with the word SHARE. His grandmother knocked while he was still looking at it. She was carrying her tablet in both hands, like a tray.

"That's today," she said. "Terrible. My cousin Elena lives there. Should I send it to her, so she knows to be careful?"

Michael said he didn't know. He said this honestly, which surprised him, because a month ago he would have said sure, send it, the way you pat someone's shoulder. But last week he had shared a clip of a riot that turned out to be three years old and from a different country, and Ben had spent an entire lunch period being voluble about it, not cruel, just relentless, in the way Ben was relentless about everything. Michael had laughed along and then gone home and felt stupid for a full evening, the specific stupid of someone who knew better and hadn't bothered.

"Sit down," he said, and pulled out the second chair.

He had never actually done the thing himself. He knew it existed the way he knew the swimming pool at the community centre existed, without ever having gone. There was, he was fairly sure, a way to make the search engine look for the picture itself instead of words. He opened the browser, typed the words he half remembered, and there it was: search by image. Google had added it back in 2011, the little summary said, long enough ago that Michael had been in kindergarten. You could upload a picture, or paste its link, and it would find where else that picture appeared on the web.

"That's it?" his grandmother said, peering. "You put the picture in the box where the words go?"

He dragged the file into the box. The wheel spun. It felt momentarily exhilarating, in the small way things do when they work on the first try, and then the results loaded and the feeling flattened into something more ordinary.

The photo was real, in the sense that it existed. It had appeared on news sites first in 2013, after a typhoon, in a country eleven hundred miles from where the caption claimed. It had resurfaced in 2016 for a different flood, in 2019 for another one, and now here, wearing today's date. His grandmother read the results slowly, her finger moving along the screen, the way she read the lottery numbers.

"So Elena," she said, "is fine."

"Elena is probably fine. This picture isn't about Elena."

She looked at him for a moment with an expression he couldn't file anywhere, and then she did the thing that made the whole evening worth it: she picked up the tablet, brought up the shark on the flooded highway, and held it out to him. "Do this one."

He did. The shark was from a 2011 magazine shoot. She made a small noise, not quite a laugh. Then she made him do the soldier, and the politician, and by the fourth one she was doing it herself, slowly, dragging with one finger, frowning at the box where the picture went. When the results came back she read them aloud, and she was quieter than he had ever heard her, quieter than at funerals.

"You're a savant," she said at last, leaning back.

"I googled it, Grandma."

"A savant with a sour face." She stood, tucked the tablet under her arm, and paused at the door. "Tomorrow you'll teach me the email again. The part where I delete things." She was already halfway up the stairs, calling back down without turning around, "And I'm sending Elena a real message. With words I wrote myself."

activity: to debate whether an ancient religious rule still applies in modern life using the text itself
knowledge_domain: to debate whether an ancient religious rule still applies in modern life using the text itself
fact: The Mishnah lists 39 categories of work forbidden on the Sabbath, which the rabbis linked to the kinds of work used to build the Tabernacle.
story:
The synagogue library smelled of dust and old glue, and the light through the high windows had gone the color of weak tea by the time Morgan found the shelf Mr. Gagnon had mentioned. He taught humanities at her school and ran the debate club, and he had said only, "If you're going to argue about Shabbat, argue from the Mishnah, not from your feelings," before handing her a call number on a scrap of paper. He had not said anything further, which she understood as the point.

Ariane was already at the long table with her laptop open, chewing the end of a pen. Their debate was in five days, and the resolution was one Mr. Gagnon had chosen deliberately: that switching on a phone counts as work forbidden on the Sabbath. Ariane had drawn the negative and wanted the win badly enough that she had printed out rebuttals and color-coded them. "You're going to lose on emotion," she said, without looking up. "You always do. You get up there and talk about meaning."

"Meaning is allowed," Morgan said, sliding the volume toward her. It was heavier than she expected, its pages soft as cloth. Hiba arrived a minute later, breathless from the bus, and dropped into the third chair with her backpack still on.

"So are we actually reading it, or are we Googling it," Hiba said.

"Reading it." Morgan turned pages until she found the chapter, and there it was, plainly, in a translation she could follow. The Mishnah lists thirty-nine categories of work forbidden on the Sabbath. She read the line aloud, then the line after it, and stopped. "It says the rabbis linked them to the kinds of work used to build the Tabernacle."

"So they're not just random rules," Hiba said slowly, leaning over. "They all come from one thing."

"That's why there are so many of them. They're all related, like a family." Morgan hesitated over the word that came to her, then said it anyway. "There's a kind of consanguinity. They share the same parent."

Ariane pulled the book toward herself and scanned the list, running her pen down the margin. Carrying, burning, writing, tearing, sewing. Nowhere did a phone appear, and nowhere did electricity, because the text was old, older than any of the things Morgan wanted to defend or condemn. That was the problem, and she could feel the debate rearranging itself around it. "See," Ariane said, tapping the page. "No phones. Negative wins."

"That's not how it works, though." Morgan said it before she had fully thought it, then made herself think it. The rabbis had taken a principle from their own past and stretched it over new cases; that was what the list was for, a set of ancestors from whom later rules could be descended. She could not just cite the list and stop, and she could not just historicize it, wave it away as a document of its moment with nothing to say to hers. Either move would be lazy. The harder position was that the categories were a method, not a museum.

"We can historicize anything into irrelevance," Hiba said, as if following the same turn of thought. "My grandmother's recipes, half of Tunis. It doesn't make the bread taste worse."

"The phone is the test, though." Ariane closed her laptop, which was her way of conceding the argument had gotten interesting. "If you press a button and something happens a mile away, is that building something? Completing a circuit? Is a circuit a thing?" She was not mocking; she genuinely wanted to know, and Morgan realized that Ariane's want and her own were the same want wearing different clothes.

They worked until the custodian's keys sounded in the hall. The commentary around the Mishnah lay in sedimentary layers, page beneath page, generations of readers pressing their questions down onto the same few lines, and Morgan copied out the passage about the Tabernacle in her own handwriting because it seemed right that her argument should begin with ink. She still did not know which side of the resolution she believed. She knew the thirty-nine categories were rooted in the work of building the sanctuary, she knew a phone pressed none of the tools of that building into anyone's hands, and she knew the rabbis had never met a question they thought was too new to answer.

At the door, Hiba zipped her backpack and said, "Saturday morning, my place, and bring the book."

"Shabbat, technically," Ariane said. "You want me to argue about the Sabbath on the Sabbath?"

Morgan held the Mishnah against her chest and said, "Bring your phone, and don't turn it on."

activity: to temper chocolate so it sets shiny and snaps cleanly
knowledge_domain: to temper chocolate so it sets shiny and snaps cleanly
fact: Cocoa butter can crystallize in six different forms, and tempering aims to make most of it set in form V, the crystal form that gives shine and snap.
story:
The kitchen at Emma-Rose's house was spartan compared with what James had imagined, a single scale, a steel bowl, a thermometer clipped to the pot like a bird clinging to a branch. He had expected equipment, machines, some professional apparatus. Instead there was only chocolate, a bag of dark couverture drops, and a problem: two bars from last week's attempt sat on the counter, dull as river stones, one of them blooming white at the edges where it had been left near the window.

"They looked like that when I unmolded them," Emma-Rose said. "Not after. I checked." She had plans for these bars, a table at the winter market where she intended to sell them in paper sleeves with a stamp her uncle had cut for her, and she wanted them perfect before she asked anyone for money. James had offered to help because he wanted to understand why chocolate worked, or failed to work, and because she had asked him first, which meant something whether he admitted it or not.

He had his phone propped against the flour canister, a page open from a pastry manual. "Listen to this," he said. "Cocoa butter can crystallize in six different forms." He read it twice, because the number surprised him. Six ways for the same fat to solidify, and only one of them was worth having. The page called it form V. Tempering, the manual said, was the whole art of getting most of the butter to set as form V, the form that gave shine and snap.

"Then that's what we did wrong," Emma-Rose said. "We let it pick its own."

"Basically, yeah."

The method was simpler than the theory. Melt the chocolate hot enough to erase every crystal it had, then cool it while working it, seeding it with a handful of solid drops so the right crystals had something to copy, then hold it in a narrow range of warmth while you poured. It felt like an argument between control and surrender. You couldn't force the crystals. You could only clear away the wrong ones and then stand there, moving the chocolate, waiting for the right ones to choose themselves. James thought of his physics teacher's distinction between states you can impose and states a system falls into, and how the second kind always seemed to require more patience, not less.

He melted the chocolate to forty-five degrees, watching the thermometer's line crawl, then pulled the bowl off the heat and began adding the seed drops a few at a time, stirring slow figures of eight with a spatula. Emma-Rose hovered with her own thermometer and called out numbers like a coach calling splits. At thirty-one degrees the chocolate on the spatula began to thicken, and the manual said hold it there, don't let it drop further, don't let it climb. James understood suddenly that tempering was not a trick or a secret but a maintenance, a constant small correction, like keeping a bicycle upright. The moment you stopped steering you began to fall.

"The thing I keep thinking," he said, still stirring, "is whether this counts as natural or not. Like it's just fat doing what fat does. But we're steering it."

"You could say that about bread," Emma-Rose said. "Or about us, honestly. School steers us."

"That's different." He wasn't sure it was. The shine they were chasing was, in a sense, an artifice, a manufactured arrangement of fat crystals that would never occur on its own in a warm kitchen, and yet every step of it was only encouraging something the chocolate already contained. He found he couldn't cleanly separate the two ideas, and said so, and Emma-Rose shrugged and said that maybe that was the point of learning anything, that it refused to sort itself politely.

He dipped the tip of a knife and set the smear on parchment, waiting five seconds before it hardened with a dry, clean sound when he flexed it. Snap. Not bend, not smear. Both of them heard it and neither said anything for a moment, the way you don't speak too soon after something lands. He poured the tempered chocolate into Emma-Rose's molds, tapping the tray flat against the counter to chase out the air, and they carried it to the cool landing at the top of the basement stairs, a place with no drafts and no radiators, and left it there, and went back to the kitchen to wash the bowls and not talk about how long twenty minutes could feel.

When they peeled the first bar from the mold it came away with a surface like a still pond at dusk, dark and uniform, and when Emma-Rose broke a corner off it made the sound again, sharp and decisive, a sound the dull bars from last week could never have made. She held the bar up to the window light and turned it once. "People will pay for this," she said, half a question, and James understood she was asking something larger than whether the market table would work, whether the thing she loved could be sold without being cheapened, whether making bars for money commodified them or simply fed the making of more bars. He didn't have the answer, so he took the piece she offered him and put it in his mouth and let it melt against his tongue while she wrapped the rest in paper sleeves, pressing the stamp down hard on each one.

activity: to read a short news article in a new language and summarise it aloud
knowledge_domain: to read a short news article in a new language and summarise it aloud
fact: Most news articles use the 'inverted pyramid': the most important facts come first and less important details follow, so the opening paragraph carries the core story.
story:
The café in Oaxaca had one fan turning overhead, and Tyler had arranged his notebook, his dictionary, and the newspaper as if the arrangement itself were a kind of prayer. His father had left him there for the morning with a task that felt, at first, like a punishment: find a short article in Spanish, read it, and be ready to summarise it aloud for the family at dinner. His Spanish was two years of classroom drills, good for ordering food and useless for a newspaper, which seemed to be written by people in a hurry for people who were also in a hurry. He had chosen the shortest article he could find, three paragraphs about a farmers' dispute over water, and he had begun, naturally, at the beginning, which was where the trouble started.

The first paragraph resisted him like a locked door. He looked up half the words before he understood half the sentence. "Dispute," he got. "Reservoir," he got eventually. But the sentence kept spiraling, clause after clause, and after forty minutes he had decoded perhaps two lines and retained nothing. Frustrated, he flipped his attention to the final paragraph, which was shorter, hoping for an easier entry point. That paragraph turned out to be about a forthcoming municipal meeting, which was easier to translate but seemed to belong to some other story entirely. He could not tell how the meeting connected to the reservoir, and he had the sinking feeling he was assembling a puzzle from the bottom.

Mr. Pérez, who owned the pension next door and took his coffee at the same café every morning at the same diurnal hour, watched Tyler wage his campaign against the third paragraph with visible sympathy. He was a retired schoolteacher with a connoisseur's interest in difficult students, and he had already decided, Tyler suspected, that Tyler was one of his interesting cases. "You read like a man eating a fish starting at the tail," he said in slow, deliberate Spanish. "Why?"

Tyler explained, in his careful, plodding way, that the last paragraph was the shortest one. Mr. Pérez laughed, then tapped the first paragraph with one finger. "Not because it is small," he said. "Because it is the whole story. Most news articles use the inverted pyramid. The most important facts come first." He spread his hands, wide at the top, narrowing down. "Everything after is less important. The opening paragraph carries the core. You wasted your time down there." He said it without cruelty, but Tyler felt it anyway, the small denigration of an hour's labor, accurate and therefore worse.

They worked the first paragraph together then, Mr. Pérez refusing to translate whole sentences, offering only single words when Tyler stalled. And with that guidance the paragraph began to yield. The core of the story, it turned out, was entirely there: who was disputing, over what, and what had happened so far. The middle paragraph added background, old grievances and prior negotiations. The last paragraph, the one Tyler had chewed on first, was merely the least important detail, a note about what might come next. When he pushed the paper away, his hand ached from writing and his pride ached from the wasted hour, but he had something he had not had that morning: he could say what the article was about.

While Mr. Pérez paid for his coffee, Tyler took out his phone and typed a message to Leanna, who was spending her summer doing something sensible and American, like lifeguarding, and who had promised to quiz him on his trip. "You were right that I'd complain," he wrote. "But listen. I spent an hour on the last paragraph of a Spanish article because it was short, and it turns out the whole story was in the first one the entire time. There's a name for it. Inverted pyramid. Most important facts first, less important stuff after. I felt like an idiot and then like a genius in the same hour, which might just be what learning is." Her reply came while he was still staring at his own message: "You learned it the hard way, which is the only way you learn anything. Send me the article. I want to see the pyramid."

Dinner that night was at a long communal table at the market, his parents and his younger sister and paper plates of mole. When his father nodded at him, the arranged signal, Tyler laid the folded newspaper beside his plate and began to speak. His summary came out slow and imperfect, the verbs arriving sometimes in the wrong tense, and twice he had to stop and search for a word while his sister smirked. But he delivered the core of the article first, cleanly, who and what and why, and only then, when his father's eyebrows rose in genuine surprise, did he add the background and the note about the meeting. He watched his family take it in the way readers of newspapers do, most first, least last.

Afterward, walking back through the streets toward the pension, he thought about messaging Mr. Pérez a thank you and could not find the words in either language. There was something he could not yet name about the morning: that the trick had worked, and that the trick was also a kind of loss, because now every article he read would be a solved problem rather than a locked door, and he had liked, in some stubborn part of himself, the locked doors. His father clapped him on the shoulder once, wordless, and his sister ran ahead toward a woman selling churros, and Tyler stopped at the corner where the café's lights still burned yellow through the glass. Mr. Pérez was there, alone now at his small table, folded newspaper before him, reading, Tyler noticed, from the very top.

activity: to analyse an unreliable narrator in a novel and how the point of view shapes the reader's trust
knowledge_domain: to analyse an unreliable narrator in a novel and how the point of view shapes the reader's trust
fact: In The Great Gatsby, published in 1925, the narrator Nick Carraway says, 'I am one of the few honest people that I have ever known.'
story:
The bus smelled of wet raincoats and diesel, and Paige had claimed the seat behind the rear wheel well because it jolted hardest and therefore kept her awake. She held the paperback open at an angle, one thumb pinning the page against the seat in front of her, and read the sentence for the third time. "I am one of the few honest people that I have ever known." Nick Carraway, a man who had spent the entire novel watching a lie and taking notes on it for later.

Rishi dropped into the seat across the aisle with his own copy held shut by a rubber band. "Ms. Oliveira wants two pages on him by Friday," he said. "On Nick. I don't get the assignment. He's the narrator. Isn't he just, like, the camera?"

"Cameras don't say things like that about themselves," Paige said. She tapped the page. "This is The Great Gatsby, it came out in 1925, and here's Nick telling us, straight out, that he's one of the few honest people he's ever known."

"So he's honest. Great. Two pages, done."

But it was not done, and the torpid sway of the bus over the pothole by the mail sorting depot seemed to argue her point for her, rocking the book in her hands like something not to be trusted. She flipped back to the beginning, where Nick claimed he reserved all judgments, and then forward to the party where he had clearly judged everyone in the room within two paragraphs. Somewhere between those two pages a version of Nick existed that only Nick got to describe.

Alayna leaned over the seat from behind them, headphones hanging off one ear. "Are you two doing the Oliveira essay? Because I made a list." She produced a torn sheet of notebook paper, folded twice, softened at the creases. "Every time Nick says something and then does the opposite. He says he reserves judgments, and then he judges. He says he's honest, and then he doesn't tell Daisy that the woman in the car with Gatsby was her husband's mistress. He watches Tom hand out lies like hors d'oeuvres and writes them all down in his little Midwest notebook and says nothing."

"That's a lot of notebook," Rishi said.

"It's a lot of lies." Alayna smoothed the list on her knee. "I kept adding to it during fourth period. The margins ran out."

Paige took the list and read it while the bus hissed to a stop at the corner by the pharmacy and two freshmen shouldered past with their instruments. The list was longer than she expected, and it made her uneasy in a way she could not immediately place, because she had liked Nick. She had trusted him without deciding to, the way you trust whoever is driving.

"Okay," she said slowly. "So here's the problem. If the whole book is him talking, and he bends things, then everything we think we know about Gatsby came through him. The green light, the parties, all of it. We're not reading the story. We're reading Nick's version of the story."

"So the essay is, Nick is a liar, the end," Rishi said.

"No, because that's too easy." She was working it out as she said it, watching the strip mall slide past the window. "He's not lying exactly. He's choosing. He leaves things out and calls himself honest, and we believe him because he's the only voice we've got. Maybe that's the point. Maybe Fitzgerald wants us to catch it." She paused, aware she was halfway to a thesis and not sure the second half would hold. "Or maybe Nick believes his own claim. That part I can't prove either way."

Alayna said, "Ms. Oliveira would call that a strong consideration of competing interpretations."

"She called my last essay 'ambitious but torpid,'" Rishi said. "I had to look up torpid."

"You are torpid," Alayna said. "You sleep through first period."

"The word was unnecessary."

Paige was only half listening. She had turned back to the claim itself, the sentence sitting there on the page like a man introducing himself at a party with his hand already slightly behind his back. She thought about her own list of moments from the weekend, the version of Saturday she had given her mother, trimmed of the part with the fire escape. Everyone curates. That did not make every narrator a liar, and it did not make Nick one either, but it did mean the claim deserved squinting at. She could write two pages on the squinting. She could admit, on the last page, that whether Nick knew he was doing it was a question the book refused to answer, and that she was willing to leave it in that shape.

The bus swung into the school loop, and the three of them stood early, wrestling bags from the overhead rack while the driver called out for everyone to stay seated, everyone in the aisle ignoring him with the discipline of long practice.

"Your perspicacity is showing," Alayna said, nodding at the list in Paige's hand.

"I'm keeping the list," Paige said. She folded it along Alayna's soft creases and tucked it into her copy, between the lie and the claim.

Rishi rubber-banded his book shut and said, "So what do I write?"

"Write about the hand behind the back," Paige said, and stepped down into the rain.

activity: to compare two apartment leases and work out the total monthly cost including utilities
knowledge_domain: to compare two apartment leases and work out the total monthly cost including utilities
fact: In Ontario, when a fixed-term lease ends, the tenant does not have to sign a new one; the tenancy continues month to month automatically on the same terms.
story:
The two leases lay side by side on Jessica's knees, and the wind kept lifting the corner of the newer one toward the gutter. She pressed it flat with her palm. The 61 bus was twelve minutes away, which meant she had twelve minutes to decide whether she and Laurel could afford the place on Claremont before the property manager called at five, and five o'clock was non-negotiable because another couple had a viewing at six.

Laurel sat beside her on the bench, scrolling through a hydro calculator on her phone. "Okay, so Claremont says utilities aren't included, and the Galloway place says heat and water are. But Galloway is forty dollars more a month in rent, so is that actually better or worse?" She held the screen out. "I can't tell if I'm doing this right."

Jessica did the arithmetic in the margin of the Claremont lease, in pencil, twice. Galloway at eleven eighty with utilities bundled, versus Claremont at eleven forty plus hydro, plus water, plus whatever internet cost split two ways. Her grandmother, who read every scrap of paper that crossed her kitchen table, would have circled the small print in red. Jessica circled it herself: Claremont was a fixed-term lease, twelve months, and at the bottom a clause saying that at the end of the term the tenancy terminated unless renewed. She'd underlined it without thinking, the way her grandmother underlined things.

"That clause is wrong," said a voice to her left. Ms. Cohen, who taught chemistry at the high school and apparently waited at this same stop every Tuesday, was peering over with the frank interest of someone who had no intention of pretending not to. "Not wrong for you, wrong legally. My sister spent a year fighting her landlord about that exact wording."

Jessica turned the page toward her. "Fighting how?"

"Your grandmother would know it better than I do," Ms. Cohen said, which was true, since her grandmother had resuscitated more than one of Jessica's crises with a phone call to the tenant hotline. "But the way I understand it, when a fixed-term lease ends here, you don't have to sign a new one. The tenancy just continues month to month on the same terms, whether the landlord likes it or not."

Laurel looked up from the hydro calculator. "So the termination clause is decoration?"

"Decorative," Ms. Cohen agreed, and the bus appeared at the far corner before anyone could say more, its front end looming turgid and silver through the heat shimmer off the asphalt.

On the bus, Jessica laid the leases across both their laps and started again, but differently now. Darian slid into the seat across the aisle, back from his appointment at the allergy clinic, rubbing his shoulder and complaining that the antigen injections made his arm feel like a ham for two days afterward. He glanced at the papers without being asked. "Moving in together, finally? Laurel, you said the Galloway guy wanted a year commitment in writing."

"That's the thing," Laurel said. "He does. He sent a renewal form for next year already, this year hasn't even started."

Jessica tapped the Claremont page with her pencil. Her grandmother had said almost the same thing last Sunday, waving the phone at the landlord on the other end of the line, telling him not to worry her with renewal paperwork because no new lease was needed, the month-to-month just carries on. Jessica had half listened, assuming it was one of her grandmother's certainties, the kind that sounded like law and might be only opinion. Now it had come at her from two directions in one afternoon. She wrote Galloway: 1180, everything in, renew or leave. Claremont: 1140 plus utilities, month to month after the term whether they sign or not. Then, because Laurel hated hidden numbers, she added a rough hydro estimate for a second-floor unit with old windows, and watched the totals slide toward each other until Claremont lost its advantage entirely.

"So they cost nearly the same," Laurel said slowly. "But one of them we can leave with two months' notice after the year, and one of them we'd have to negotiate our way out of."

"Or stay in without renegotiating," Jessica said. "Which is what he's counting on us not knowing."

The property manager hadn't said anything untrue; he'd only let the clause sit there like a fact. Jessica understood, looking at her own circled underline, that she'd almost signed it as one. What she still couldn't know, and said so, was whether the Claremont landlord was careless or counting on it, and whether it mattered, given that the two places cost the same and Galloway had the newer kitchen. Laurel was already dialing. "It's four forty," she said, holding the phone between them. "Ask him about the clause before we say anything. Let him hear that we know."

Jessica took the phone, and when the line picked up, she read the clause aloud, flat, without a question mark anywhere in her voice.

activity: to lead a holiday meal ceremony from start to finish for the whole family
knowledge_domain: to lead a holiday meal ceremony from start to finish for the whole family
fact: Charoset, a sweet paste of chopped fruit and nuts on the Seder plate, represents the mortar the enslaved Israelites used to lay bricks in Egypt.
story:
Charles commandeered the kitchen at four o'clock, moving his mother's usual things to the counter's far end: the coffee maker, the mail, the bowl of dying tangerines. His grandmother's Haggadah lay open at the Seder plate diagram, and he kept glancing at it the way a student glances at a cheat sheet he is no longer sure he understands. Tonight he would lead the whole meal. His father had said it lightly, at dinner two weeks ago, the way you hand someone a set of car keys. You're eighteen. You know the words better than I do now. Charles had not argued, which was its own kind of mistake.

Stefal came over at five with a bag of walnuts and no other plans, which was Stefan's way of being loyal. He sat on the counter stool and watched Charles chop apples with more force than the apples required. "You're going to saw through the board," Stefan said. Charles didn't answer. The apples had to be right. Everything had to be right, and he had discovered at three in the morning that he could recite the Four Questions since he was six but could not say, if someone asked, why there was a bowl of sweet brown paste on the Seder plate at all.

Khalil arrived with his little sister's science project poster board, which he was storing at Charles's house for reasons he declined to explain, and immediately began eating the raisins Charles had set aside. "It's called charoset," Charles said, moving the bowl out of reach. "That's the one thing I know." Khalil shrugged, stoic, and kept eating from the bag in his hand instead. Charles grated the apples into the bowl, folded in the walnuts and wine and cinnamon, and the smell of it rose up sharp and sweet, the exact smell of every Passover he could remember, and he still could not have told you what it was for.

He texted Mr. Smith, who had been his tenth grade history teacher and who answered questions on weekends like a man who missed having questions to answer. What's on the Seder plate that's sweet? Mr. Smith replied within a minute, which was almost suspicious. Then a second message: the charoset. It stands for the mortar. The enslaved Israelites laid bricks in Egypt, and the paste is mortar. Charles read it twice. Mortar. He looked at the bowl, at the glistening chopped fruit and nuts he had just made, and felt something turn over in him. A sweet thing standing for a bitter labor. The same plate held bitter herbs and salt water and this, and now he couldn't decide whether the sweetness was comfort or irony.

His father came into the kitchen at six, taciturn from work, loosening his tie. He stood beside Charles and looked at the plate Charles had assembled, all six items in their places, and something in his face softened, though he only said, "You used the good wine." "For the charoset," Charles said. "It's mortar," his father said, not a question. "Grandpa used to say, we eat the bricks." Charles realized his father had known this his whole life and had never once said it out loud at a Seder, the same way his grandfather hadn't, or maybe had, in years Charles was too young to remember.

They argued, briefly, about the order of the evening. Charles wanted to add a paragraph he'd written himself, something about the mortar, about sweetness and slavery sitting on the same plate, and his father said that people were arriving at six thirty and the soup wasn't on. "It's one minute of reading," Charles said. His father looked at him for a long moment, and Charles understood that the argument wasn't about the paragraph, it was about who got to decide what the ceremony was for, and that this was the actual beginning of leading it, this uncomfortable minute, not the candles or the wine or the questions later.

The aunts and uncles filled the kitchen by seven, and Stefan and Khalil were folded into the table like cousins, and Charles stood up with the Haggadah in his hands and his mouth dry. He read the blessings he had known since childhood, and his voice only shook a little. When they reached the Seder plate, his youngest cousin pointed at the brown paste and asked what it was, the question Charles had been unable to answer that morning, and Charles said, "That's charoset. It stands for the mortar the enslaved Israelites used to lay bricks in Egypt." The table went quiet in the way it does when a familiar thing is said by an unfamiliar voice. His grandmother, three seats down, nodded once.

He didn't read his paragraph. He left it folded in his pocket, and he couldn't have said whether that was mercy or cowardice, and he suspected he would still be deciding in a year. Later, when the guests had thinned to the ones who stayed for the cold cuts, Charles found Stefan and Khalil in the kitchen eating what was left of the charoset with spoons, straight from the bowl. "So it's bricks," Khalil said. "Bricks you want to eat." Charles took the second spoon from the drawer and sat down with them. "Pass it here," he said.

activity: to critique a painting by Frida Kahlo using formal analysis of colour, composition and symbolism
knowledge_domain: to critique a painting by Frida Kahlo using formal analysis of colour, composition and symbolism
fact: Complementary colours sit opposite each other on the traditional colour wheel, like red and green, and placed side by side they make each other look brighter.
story:
Austin had spread his mother's print of Frida Kahlo's self-portrait with thorn necklace across the kitchen table, next to a cereal bowl he had not cleared and a library book called Looking at Pictures, which was three weeks overdue. Ms. Iyer wanted eight hundred words by Friday on colour, composition and symbolism, and so far he had written one sentence, deleted it, and written it again.

Oskar arrived at four with his own agenda, which was not art. He had a history essay on the Cold War due Thursday, and the Iyers' house had better wifi, but their kitchen had been full of his little sisters, so he had walked the extra two blocks to Austin's, holding his laptop like a pizza box. He sat down across from Austin and opened it.

"Don't look at me like that," Austin said. "It's not even due till Friday."

"It's due Friday and you've written nothing."

"I've written a sentence." He turned the laptop so Oskar could see. The cursor blinked at the top of an otherwise empty page. "The problem is Ms. Iyer keeps saying the painting is a statement about suffering, and I don't want to just say that back to her. She said anyone who turns in a summary of Kahlo's biography gets marked down. She wants us to look at the actual paint."

Oskar, who could be loquacious when he'd had a good day at school, was quiet now, chewing the end of a pen. His Cold War essay sat half finished on his own screen. Finally he leaned over the table and frowned at the print. "Why does her face look like it's lit from a TV?"

Austin looked. The jungle behind Kahlo was green, wet green, leaf after leaf of it, and the thorns at her throat were drawn in a red so deep it was almost blood. Where the red touched the green it seemed to hum. He pulled the library book toward him and turned to the chapter on colour, which he had skipped because it looked like homework.
