His mother had grown up in El Paso with one grandmother who kept the traditions and one who called them superstition, and Chase had, without deciding to, acceded to the second grandmother's view, the tidy skeptical one, the one that didn't require believing anything. His grandfather himself had been the quietest kind of nonbeliever, a man who fixed carburetors and read the weather and said, when Chase's dog died, that being gone meant being gone.

But he was the one holding the photograph, and the photograph was heavier than paper should be, and his mother was unwrapping the marigolds now, snapping the stems to the right length with a competence he hadn't known she had. "You're supposed to be able to smell them from the door," she said. "That's the point. A strong scent. He finds his way by it." She said it lightly, the way she said things that weren't light.

"Do you actually believe that," Chase asked. "That he comes back?"

She didn't stop working. She set the flowers in a jar of water and turned the jar until the best blooms faced the room, and there was a subtlety in how she did it, an attention he associated with her arranging a family argument so that nobody lost face. "I believe we miss him," she said. "I believe this is a way to miss him out loud instead of in my head all day. If he comes, good. If he doesn't, the house still smells like his garden." She paused. "You could put the photo somewhere, if you want. I wasn't going to ask you."

He had been ready to say that he didn't want to, that it felt like performing something he didn't feel, and now the sentence wouldn't assemble itself. He thought of Mckenna's message again, That's what people believe anyway, the anyway doing more work than she probably intended. Maybe belief wasn't a door you walked through or didn't. Maybe it was a door you stood near. His grandfather would have laughed at the flowers, but he would also have stayed up late sitting beside them, because his wife's daughter had made them, and that was the arithmetic he lived by.

Chase placed the photograph at the center of the shelf, above the candles, and adjusted it twice. The orange of the marigolds caught the light and threw it back warmer than the room deserved. He thought, absurdly, of a runway at night, of something bright laid out on purpose so that someone could find the way down, and he couldn't tell whether the thought was his own skepticism turned gentle or the beginning of the other thing, and he decided he was allowed not to know.

"You're supposed to put out things he liked," his mother said from the kitchen. "Food. Anything."

"Music," Chase said. "He faked playing guitar for forty years." He went to his room and came back with his own guitar, the one his grandfather had restrung for him two birthdays ago, the last time his hands were steady enough for the small strings. He leaned it against the shelf beside the marigolds, and the neck angled up toward the photograph like something mid-gesture, and he stood there a while with the candles unlit because his mother had the matches.

Two days later, on the second of November, Mckenna texted him a picture of marigolds from her aunt's house and asked if the thing with his mom had worked. Chase looked at the ofrenda across the room, the flowers browning only slightly at the edges, still bright enough to be unmistakable. "Come over," he said to his mother, before he could think better of it. "Come see it before the days are over."

activity: getting a first part-time job
knowledge_domain: getting a first part-time job
fact: In the United States, every new employee must complete Section 1 of Form I-9, which verifies identity and permission to work, no later than their first day of paid work.
story:
Victoria found the email at eleven at night, screen-lit in her dark bedroom: orientation Saturday, nine a.m., bring identification. The bookstore had hired her over the phone, and she had said yes before thinking about what yes required. She read the line twice, then texted Flora, who was also job hunting.

Flora answered with a shrug emoji and "bring ur passport i guess." Coraly, brought into the group chat, said her cousin had been sent home from a bakery for missing paperwork, though the details were vague and possibly invented. Victoria did not own a passport. She went downstairs and asked her mother where the birth certificate was, and her mother said something about the filing cabinet that did not augur well for Saturday morning.

Saturday she arrived at nine with a folder: birth certificate, social security card, a utility bill with her name on it from when she had opened a library account. The manager, a tired man with a lanyard, handed her a clipboard across the counter. "You need to complete Section 1 of Form I-9 before you start today," he said. "It verifies identity and permission to work. Everyone does it, no later than their first day of paid work."

"I brought documents," Victoria said, and laid them out like a hand of cards.

He looked at the utility bill and slid it back. "That one's not for Section 1." He tapped the form. "This part's yours. Today."

The form was two pages and strange. Citizenship status. A signature box with a warning underneath about perjury. She had filled out college applications for months, essays and activity lists, and none of it had felt like this, her identity reduced to checkboxes that had legal weight. Behind her, a boy about her age waited for his own clipboard, bouncing on his heels. "First job?" he asked. "Mine too. My mom made me practice signing."

She almost laughed, and the laugh helped. She completed the boxes, printed her name where it said print, signed where it said sign, and chose her document in the little grid. The manager checked the social security card against what she had written, turning it in the light like a jeweler. Then he initialed something and the whole thing vanished into a folder behind the register, and that was it. She was legal, employable, ordinary.

Her first shift was shelving returns. Somewhere between biography and cooking she understood that she had walked in with two ideas of herself and only one had survived the morning: the Victoria of the personal essay, who could argue both sides of anything, and the Victoria of the form, who had checked a single box in pen. Both had felt true. Only one had a signature and a date. She was honest enough with herself to admit that she did not know yet which one would be doing the living this summer, or whether a person could keep a foot in each without being dishonest on some future form she had not yet met.

At her break, Flora texted a photo of a hiring email from a coffee shop. "what do i bring??" Victoria typed the answer carefully, the whole thing, Section 1 of Form I-9, first day of paid work, no later. Then she deleted the lecture she had started to add about being prepared, because she had not been prepared either, and sent instead: "bring documents. i'll come with you. i get a discount on muffins now."

There was a pause, then Flora replied, "wait you got employee discount already? i'm applying there instead."

Victoria put the phone in her apron pocket and went back to the cart of returns. On top of the pile sat a cookbook she had shelved wrong an hour ago, dog-eared by some stranger, and she picked it up to do it right this time.

activity: to argue both sides of a Supreme Court case about free speech before a mock court
knowledge_domain: to argue both sides of a Supreme Court case about free speech before a mock court
fact: Schenck v. United States introduced the 'clear and present danger' test, allowing speech to be punished if it created a clear and present danger of harm Congress could prevent.
story:
The marble stairs of city hall were still wet from the morning's rain, and Emily climbed them with her outline cards sweating against her palm. Inside, the council chamber had been rearranged into something like a courtroom, three desks pushed to the front for the judges, a lectern in the middle, folding chairs in rows behind. Mr. Aydın was stacking the case files on the end desk, and Sierra was already there, leaning against the rail that separated the gallery from the floor, looking nonchalant in a way Emily knew cost her something.

"You drew both sides," Sierra said. "I heard Mr. Aydın tell the clerk. You argue for Schenck first, then you turn around and argue for the United States."

"Both sides," Emily said. "Same case. Free speech against the Espionage Act."

"So you have to beat yourself." Sierra smiled, but not all the way. They had been friends since the sophomore debate team, and then not exactly friends, and then something with no name, two people who kept checking each other's tournament results. "That's either the best assignment in the room or the worst."

Emily did not answer, because she didn't know. She had spent two weeks trying to love the government's case, the one where Charles Schenck went to prison for printing leaflets telling drafted soldiers to resist, and every draft she wrote sounded like she was apologizing between sentences. Then she would flip to the other outline and feel the opposite problem, that defending the leaflets was so easy it felt like cheating.

The clerk called the case, and the students who weren't arguing filled the gallery chairs with their coats and their phones. Mr. Aydın sat in the middle seat and adjusted the microphone, which squealed once and then went quiet.

Emily rose for the petitioner first. She laid out the speech claim, the First Amendment, the leaflets as opinion, and she was building toward the danger argument she knew was coming when she heard herself say it early, unguarded, testing it: that some speech could be punished if it created a clear and present danger of a harm Congress could prevent. She had found the test in the case itself, in the majority opinion she'd read four times on the bus, underlining until the pen went through the page. Saying it aloud in the chamber, with the flags on either side of the dais, she felt the words shift shape. They sounded reasonable. They sounded like something that could swallow everything.

"That's the government's test," Mr. Aydín said from the bench, mild. "You're wearing the wrong coat, counselor."

"It's the Court's test," Emily said, and her heart knocked against her ribs. "If I'm going to argue against it, I should say it plainly first."

She finished the speech side the way she'd planned, but weaker, and when she sat down at the respondent's table and turned her cards over, the room tilted slightly. Sierra stood to cross-examine her, and beneath the questions about precedent and editorial cartoons there was a second conversation happening, the one where Sierra was asking whether Emily had meant the earlier stumble, whether it was strategy or confession. Emily answered the surface questions and let the other one go by unanswered, and Sierra's jaw tightened at the missed exchange.

For the government, Emily tried to resuscitate the danger test. She argued that a country at war could reasonably punish speech that menaced the draft, that Congress could prevent that harm, that the danger was clear and present in the leaflets themselves. But mid-sentence she saw the whole structure differently, the way two lenses clicked together in a stereoscope: the speech side was right that the test could reach too far, and the government side was right that words were not somehow weightless, that a crowd handing out resistance leaflets outside a draft office was doing something with consequences. Both of those could be true. What she could not find, in any of her cards, was the line where one truth stopped and the other started.

"Ms. Emily," Mr. Aydın said during rebuttal questions, "if the test is wrong, what replaces it? You've told us what you'd strike down. Tell me what you'd keep."

"I don't know yet," she said, and the gallery laughed a little, the cheap laugh at honesty. She waited it out. "I think punishing speech for a clear and present danger is too broad, and I think no limits at all is too blind. Somewhere between them there's a line. I can see both ends of it. Not the line."

Sierra was watching her from the rail with her arms folded, and when the clerk called time, Sierra didn't move to pack up. She crossed the little distance to the respondent's table and put her hand flat on Emily's outline cards, the government side, the ones Emily had almost believed.

"You argued my side better than I would have," Sierra said. "That's the most annoying thing anyone's ever done to me."

"Give me a week," Emily said, "and I'll argue it against you."

activity: to check a viral video's source and date with a reverse image search before sharing it
knowledge_domain: to check a viral video's source and date with a reverse image search before sharing it
fact: The SIFT method from educator Mike Caulfield stands for Stop, Investigate the source, Find better coverage, and Trace claims to their original context.
story:
The video arrived in the group chat at eleven minutes past ten, while Grace was sitting on Anjali's bedroom floor with her back against the bed and a bowl of popcorn wedged between her knees. Grainy footage, night vision green, a flooded street with what looked like a shark fin cutting through the brown water toward a stranded car. "This is downtown," Arabella had typed. "Share before they take it down." Ten people had already sent it onward, and Anjali's thumb was hovering over the resend arrow when Grace caught her wrist.

"Hold on," Grace said. "That's not downtown."

Anjali set the phone down on the carpet between them. "It's a shark in a parking garage, Grace. It doesn't have to be downtown. It just has to be real."

But that was exactly the question, and Grace felt the shape of it before she could say it well. Last month she had forwarded a clip of a hospital hallway, choked with gurneys, captioned with the name of her own city, and her mother had forwarded it to three coworkers before someone traced it to a different country, four years old, filmed during an unrelated outbreak. The memory still made her ears go hot. She had wanted to be the person who spread the alarm, and instead she had been the person who spread the mud.

"Watch," she said, and took a screenshot of the shark video, then opened a search engine and dragged the image into the little camera icon in the search bar. Anjali leaned in, smelling of the popcorn butter on her own fingers. The results loaded slowly, the way everything loaded in this house, and then a grid of matching pictures bloomed across the screen. A news site. A fact-checking page. A fishing forum from three years ago.

"That's it," Anjali said flatly. "That's the same fin."

The earliest version, dated three summers back, was attached to a story about a marine park after a hurricane, a nurse shark that had washed into a retention pond and been relocated by wildlife officers. Someone had clipped the footage, darkened it, stripped the date, and dropped it into a flooded-street video from a city that had, in fairness, actually flooded this week. The two true things had been braided into one false thing, and the braid was convincing. Grace could see why. The water in the real flood footage was turbid, brown and thick with silt, exactly like the water in her own memory of local storms, and similarity felt like proof even when it was only resemblance.

In her notebook, the one she kept for the media literacy unit that Ms. Whitaker had made optional and Grace had made personal, there was a page headed with four letters. SIFT. She'd copied it off a handout weeks ago without much caring, but now she flipped to it in her head. Stop. Investigate the source. Find better coverage. Trace claims to their original context. That was the whole thing, four moves, and she had just done the last one without naming it. "It's the SIFT method," she said aloud, mostly to fix it in place. "This guy Mike Caulfield, he's an educator, he came up with it. Stop, investigate the source, find better coverage, trace claims back to the original context." Anjali raised an eyebrow, and Grace shrugged. "It was on a handout. I thought it was going to be boring. It's not boring."

"It's four steps to kill a shark video," Anjali said.

"It's four steps to not look like an idiot," Grace said. "Same thing."

The difficulty arrived a minute later, and it was Arabella, calling through the speakerphone with the sound of a party behind her, insistent and bright. "Anj, did you share it? My cousin's in that neighborhood, we can't reach her, if there's a shark there's a bigger problem, there could be sewage, there could be anything." Grace understood then that this was not a lesson about stupidity. Arabella was not stupid. Arabella was frightened for someone she loved, and fear makes a person want a piece of information that can be acted on immediately, a shard of news that can be gripped. That was the engine underneath all of it, she thought, not malice but the appetite to help, ready to be exploited by anyone willing to strip a date off a video. The whole machinery of misinformation could not subjugate a population by force; it only had to offer each frightened person a false thing to do.

"There's no shark," Grace said toward the phone. "The fin is from a marine park in another state, three years ago. I found the original. Your cousin's neighborhood did flood, that part's real, and that's what you should check on, the actual flood warnings, not the fish."

Silence on the line, then the party noise swelling back in. "So it's fake?"

"The shark's fake. The flood's real. Both things."

Arabella hung up without saying much, which Grace decided not to read too deeply into. Anjali picked up the popcorn bowl and ate a handful, thoughtful, kernels cracking in the quiet. "She's going to be embarrassed," Anjali said.

"She'll get over it or she won't. I didn't get over it, exactly. I just got slower." Grace pulled up the group chat and began typing, deleting her first attempt, which sounded smug, and her second, which sounded like a term paper. The third one she kept. "Shark is old footage from a marine park, reverse image search will show you. Flood warnings for our area are at the county site. Check before you send." She hit post before she could soften it further, and the message sat there in the thread, small and unglamorous under ten copies of a shark.

Anjali watched it send, then tilted her phone screen toward Grace. One of the ten friends had replied with a single eye emoji, which meant nothing yet, which meant someone was looking. "Do it again," Anjali said. "Whatever that was. The four steps. Next time something shows up, do it again and tell me first."

"That's the plan," Grace said, and reached for the popcorn.

activity: to find the derivative of a polynomial function and use it to locate a maximum
knowledge_domain: to find the derivative of a polynomial function and use it to locate a maximum
fact: The notation dy/dx for a derivative comes from Gottfried Leibniz and is still standard in mathematics today.
story:
Gabrielle had the kitchen table to herself until six, which was the deal: her mother took her brother to swim practice, and the house went quiet enough to hear the refrigerator hum. The test was first period tomorrow. On the page in front of her, a polynomial squatted like a dare: f of x equals negative x cubed plus six x squared minus nine x plus two, find the maximum. She had done the practice problems in September when Ms. Tremblay walked the rows and checked each line. Now, alone, she could not remember whether she was supposed to set the derivative equal to zero or plug the endpoint in, or both, and the textbook's dense paragraphs only rearranged her confusion into fancier words.

She texted Justus, who answered with a photo of his own page, half legible, and the message "omw." He lived four streets over and never knocked; he came in calling "It's me" the way people do in houses they've been visiting since middle school. He set his bag down, looked at her page, and pulled a chair around beside her rather than across, so they could both see the same work.

"Okay," he said. "Differentiate first. What do you get?"

She wrote it out slowly, term by term, the way Ms. Tremblay had made them do at the board. Negative three x squared plus twelve x minus nine. Justus tapped the page. "Now, where's the top of the hill? What's the slope doing there?"

"Zero. Flat." She set the expression equal to zero and factored: negative three times x squared minus four x plus three, so x equals one or x equals three. One was the local minimum. Three had to be the maximum. She leaned back, almost giddy, and then leaned forward again because she still had to justify it, still had to say why three and not one.

"Wait," she said. "Why does the book write it like that? Dy over dx. Like a fraction. It's not a fraction, we're not dividing anything." She flipped to the front of the chapter and there it was again, stacked, dy on top of dx, on every page.

Justus looked at it longer than the question seemed to deserve. "My cousin said something about this. The notation, the dy over dx, it comes from Gottfried Leibniz." He traced the symbols with his pen. "And it's still the standard in math today. Everybody uses it. Newton had his own thing with dots, but this is the one that stuck."

"So we're doing homework in a dead man's handwriting."

"He'd be thrilled." Justus was only half facetious; he actually seemed to like the idea, writing in ink that hadn't dried in three hundred years. Gabrielle looked at the stacked letters and thought of her grandmother's cursive on recipe cards, the way everyone in the family still made the birthday cake in that script because retranscribing it would feel like a betrayal. The notation was an inheritance, handed down intact, and no one had contested it the way her uncles contested the cottage, arguing about primogeniture at a funeral lunch until her mother walked out.

"Fine," she said. "I'll trust the fraction that isn't a fraction." She tested x equals three in the second derivative: negative six, which meant the curve was concave down, which meant a peak. Then, to be safe, she took f of three and f of two and f of four, plotted the three points, and drew a smooth arc through them, interpolating the shape of the hill between her calculated spots. The arc peaked at three, right where the algebra said. Two roads, one drawn by hand and one by symbols, arriving at the same summit. "If I get this wrong now," she said, "it's because I want to be wrong."

Justus was not laughing. He had gone still, his pen resting against the margin of her notebook rather than his own, and she realized he had been holding his page at an angle all evening, turned slightly away. She reached over and turned it flat. His problem was blank after the first line.

"I was going to skip this question," he said. "I've been letting you talk it through so I could copy the shape of the thinking. That's not the same as having it."

From where Justus sat, the kitchen looked different than it did in his own house: a bowl of clementines within reach, a glass of water someone had poured for him without asking, a mother due back at seven who would ask whether he'd eaten and mean it. At home he had a bedroom and a microwave and parents who worked until nine. He had gotten good at seeming fine by watching how fine looked on other people and copying it. Gabrielle slid her notebook to the middle of the table where it belonged to neither of them.

"Then talk it through out loud," she said. "I'll tell you where you lose me. You have until my mom gets home with the pizza."

He picked up the pen. "Differentiate first," he said, and wrote negative three x squared plus twelve x minus nine underneath the polynomial, then stopped at the equals zero and looked at her, not the page. She waited. The refrigerator hummed. He factored, hesitated, and set the quadratic right.

"One or three," he said. "And I check the second derivative to see which one's the hill."

The headlights swept the driveway.

activity: to apply a feminist or Marxist critical lens to a passage from a classic novel
knowledge_domain: to apply a feminist or Marxist critical lens to a passage from a classic novel
fact: Marx and Engels's Communist Manifesto of 1848 opens its first section by claiming that the history of all hitherto existing society is the history of class struggles.
story:
The library meeting room smelled of carpet cleaner and old glue, and the book club had pushed the tables into the usual lopsided square. Maelle arrived last, carrying Jane Eyre with three sticky tabs bristling from its spine, because Ms. Sun had announced at the previous meeting that this month they would try reading the novel "differently," and Maelle had spent two anxious days deciding what differently meant.

"Grab a chair," said Ms. Sun, who ran the club with a kind of weary patience, as though every discussion were a cat that might scratch. Kayson was already there, flipping through a photocopy with a suspicious expression. Mikayla was eating string cheese in open defiance of the signage.

Ms. Sun had placed a stack of handouts at the center of the tables. "Feminist lens today," she said. "Or Marxist. Or both, if you're ambitious. Ask what the text does with power. Who has it, who doesn't, how the story spends it."

Maelle opened her book to her first tab, the passage where Mr. Rochester dresses as a gypsy fortune-teller to pry into Jane's feelings. She had prepared remarks. She had rehearsed them in the shower. But before she could begin, Kayson held up his photocopy and frowned at it.

"This is from the Communist Manifesto," he said. "1848. Why is it from that?"

Ms. Sun smiled in a way that invited trouble. "Read the first line."

Kayson read it aloud, slowly, like a man crossing ice: "The history of all hitherto existing society is the history of class struggles." He set the paper down. "Is that true? And what does it have to do with Jane Eyre? She marries her employer. That's not a struggle, that's a promotion."

Mikayla laughed, and Maelle felt something in her chest go warm and unhelpful, because she had been prepared to say something entirely different about the gypsy scene, and now the conversation was running down a corridor she hadn't mapped. She wanted to sound intelligent. That was the real problem. She wanted Ms. Sun to look up from her notes.

"Okay," she said, before the warmth could talk her out of it. "But look at the gypsy part. He's her employer, right, so he already has power over her job, her housing, everything. And he puts on a costume to get more. He wants her feelings without giving her any of his. That's not romantic, that's an interrogation."

"An interrogation," Mikayla repeated, delighted. "Querulous old Mr. Rochester, basically."

"Querulous is him complaining that nobody loves him while he owns the house," Maelle said, and the table laughed, and she laughed too, though she had not meant to be funny.

Kayson tapped his photocopy. "So the Manifesto line fits? Jane's whole story is class struggle? Poor governess, rich man?"

Maelle hesitated. This was where the prepared remarks would have been useful, but they suddenly seemed like a platitude she'd borrowed from a study website: love transcends class, something something. She didn't believe it, exactly. She turned pages instead of answering, hunting the passage where Jane inherits money and returns to find Rochester blinded and diminished.

"Here's the thing," she said. "When she comes back, she has money of her own and he's disabled. Everyone always says it's romantic. But the balance changed first. She only says yes when she doesn't have to say yes. So maybe the love story is real, but maybe it's only legible as a love story because the class part got evened out, and Brontë doesn't say that part out loud." She heard herself and worried it sounded like a lecture. "Or maybe that's reading too much in."

"It's not too much," said Kayson, quietly.

"It might be," said Mikayla, string cheese finished, chin on her fist. "Maybe she just loves him. People did that sometimes."

Ms. Sun, who had been taking no notes at all, folded her hands. "You don't have to pick one," she said. "The feminist reading and the class reading can hold the same page. They argue with each other a little. That's fine. Books can be crowded."

Maelle looked down at her three sticky tabs and found she could not remember what the third one was for. She peeled it off and pressed it onto a new page, the one where Jane tells Rochester she is no bird in a cage, and thought about the Manifesto line sitting on the table between them, unresolved and useful and possibly not entirely true.

"So is marriage in this book a happy ending," Kayson asked, "or is it the class struggle just going quiet?"

Maelle closed her book on her thumb. "Ask me in ten years."

Ms. Sun began stacking the handouts, and Mikayla said, "Next month can we do a book where nobody gets married," and the librarian knocked twice on the door, which meant the room was needed.

activity: to debate a current issue entirely in a new language for five minutes
knowledge_domain: to debate a current issue entirely in a new language for five minutes
fact: Code-switching is moving between two languages within one conversation; it is common among fluent bilinguals and is not by itself a sign of weak skill.
story:
The notice went up on the language lab door on a Tuesday: the spring debate exhibition would be conducted entirely in the target language, five minutes per speaker, no exceptions. Nicolas read it twice, then copied it into his planner as if writing it down might make it smaller. Spanish was his third year, good enough for essays about the environment and awkward phone calls with his uncle in Bogotá, but five minutes of argument, unbroken, in front of an audience, felt like being asked to juggle while reciting.

He started practicing that night at the kitchen table, arguing to his mother about whether the school day should start later. At the forty-second mark he stalled, and the English arrived like water finding a crack. "Es decir, the research shows that..." He caught it, restarted, stalled again. His mother slid him a cup of coffee and said nothing, which was its own kind of verdict.

The next afternoon Myra found him in the empty drama room, pacing with his index cards. She had grown up in a house where her grandmother spoke only Portuguese and her father answered in English, and she listened to his attempt for exactly one minute before holding up a hand. "You're doing something called code-switching," she said. "Moving between two languages in one conversation. My dad does it constantly." She shrugged, as if this settled the matter. "It's common among fluent bilinguals. It doesn't mean your Spanish is weak."

Nicolas wanted to argue, but the evidence was inconvenient: her father ran a dental practice in two languages and had once corrected Nicolas's subjunctive at a barbecue. Still, the rules on the door did not bend. "The exhibition doesn't allow it," he said. "Five minutes, entirely Spanish, that's the whole point."

"So stop treating the slip like a crime," Myra said. "Notice when it happens, and come back in Spanish. Don't freeze."

He thought of the previous autumn, a flashback that arrived without permission: Giulia, in their Italian class, describing her grandmother's village to Ms. Levy, sliding between the two languages so smoothly that no one reached for a red pen. Ms. Levy had simply nodded and let the mixed sentences stand, and Giulia had talked for six minutes about olive harvests and a dog named Giotto, glowing the entire time. Nicolas had assumed then that Giulia was simply better than he was. Now he sat with the possibility that the difference was not fluency but posture, that his own rigid insistence on purity was making him impermeable to the very language he was trying to absorb.

The following week he changed his method. Instead of fighting the English, he marked it, saying "aquí" each time he slipped, then deliberately rephrasing the idea in Spanish, even clumsily, even with a grammatical structure lifted straight from English syntax. Ms. Levy, who supervised the lab on Thursdays, wandered past and heard him do this three times in two minutes. "Interesting," she said, and kept walking, which did not augur disaster, though with her it was hard to be certain. By Friday, his slips had thinned from eleven per practice run to four. His argument, on whether cities should make public transit free, still sounded like a man walking upstairs in the dark, hands on both walls, but it was moving upward.

The exhibition came on a grey Wednesday, the language lab rearranged with folding chairs. Giulia sat in the second row; Myra gave him a small salute. Nicolas stood at the front, took one breath, and began. He described congestion, then pollution, then fare evasion, and at the ninety-second mark, reaching for the word for "fare," he felt the English rise in his throat. He heard himself say it anyway, "fare," and then, instead of drowning, he turned to the audience and offered, "el costo del pasaje," and continued. Later there would be two more slips, and later still the timer would run out with his final point half-delivered, its resolution uncertain, the question of who had actually won the exchange left to Ms. Levy's clipboard.

Afterward, in the corridor, Giulia fell into step beside him. "You switched," she said. "Twice. And you just kept going."

"I noticed," Nicolas said. He looked down at his index cards, soft at the corners from handling, half of them never touched. "Next time maybe once."

"Or," Giulia said, "next time you argue that switching is a feature of bilingual speech and dare them to dock you for it." She pushed open the door to the parking lot, and the cold air came in.

activity: to compute the electric field strength at a point between two charged plates
knowledge_domain: to compute the electric field strength at a point between two charged plates
fact: Between two parallel charged plates, the electric field strength equals the voltage across them divided by the distance between them, written E = V/d.
story:
The capacitor sat on the kitchen table where Anna had left it two nights ago, looking less like an instrument of science and more like a small silver sandwich: two rectangles of foil, a sheet of plastic from a binder sleeve between them, alligator clips trailing off the edges. Tomorrow was the regional fair. Tonight she still could not answer the question the physics teacher had asked when she'd presented in class, the one that had made her mouth go dry: "So what is the field actually doing in there, Anna? Numbers, not hand-waving."

She had said something about charges and energy and been wrong in several directions at once. Ms. Vargas had let her ramble for a full minute before saying, kindly, "Look it up tonight. You'll be glad you did." Which was the kind of advice that was easy to give and less easy to take at nine in the evening, with her mother reheating soup three feet away and her little brother's video game making explosion noises through the wall.

Danny had texted her a photo of his own project, a model of a hydroelectric dam that was, in his words, basically a water wheel in a Tupperware. "at least urs has actual electricity," he'd written, which was generous of him, since her electricity currently existed only as a battery and a question mark. Kaydence had been more blunt. "if the judge asks u anything with numbers u have to say something," she'd said at lunch, in the tone of someone describing a bear attack. Kaydence believed the fair was a meritocracy and that Anna was about to be meritocratically destroyed.

Anna spread her notes across the table and pushed aside a bowl her brother had abandoned, orange residue drying at the bottom. She had the battery, twelve volts, written in her lab book. She had measured the gap between the foils with a ruler that had a chipped corner: about two millimeters, which was two thousandths of a meter, a conversion she had to do twice because the first time she moved the decimal in the wrong direction and got a field that could have ionized the air itself, which even she knew was not happening in a kitchen. She remembered a diagram from a website she'd half-read, two parallel lines with arrows marching between them, and a formula half-remembered, the shape of a division.

She worked it through the way she worked everything through, which was to assume she was wrong and try to prove it. The voltage was what pushed charge onto the plates. The distance was what the push had to cross. So the field between them should be the one divided by the other. She wrote V over d, put her numbers under it, twelve divided by zero point zero zero two, and got six thousand. Volts per meter. She said it out loud to the kitchen. "Six thousand volts per meter." Her mother looked over from the stove and said, "That sounds like a lot," and Anna said, "It's not, actually," without knowing yet whether that was true.

She checked it against the diagram in her textbook, which she'd brought home under protest from the bottom of her locker. Between two parallel charged plates, the electric field strength equals the voltage across them divided by the distance between them. E equals V over d. It was exactly what she'd written, in exactly the order she'd written it, and she sat for a moment with the strange flatness of being right by accident. She'd been guessing. Guessing had worked. She didn't like not knowing which part of her brain had produced it.

She tried it the other way, because that was the test that mattered: if the gap were twice as wide with the same battery, would the field be twice as big or half? She stared at her own fraction until it told her. Divide by a bigger number, get a smaller answer. Half. Closer plates, stronger field. "That's why the plastic has to be thin," she said, and this time her mother didn't answer, and the soup started to smell like scorched onion.

Danny called at ten, ebullient, having discovered that his water wheel also functioned as a lamp if you shined a flashlight at it. She told him about the six thousand volts per meter. "Per meter of what," he said. "Of the gap between the plates," she said. "The field strength is the voltage divided by the distance. That's the whole thing." There was a pause in which she could hear him drawing it on his hand, and then he said, "Huh. Okay. Mine's a lamp."

She taped a fresh page into her lab book and copied the numbers in her best handwriting, then wrote the formula twice more, once small in the margin like a signature. Twelve volts across two millimeters, six thousand volts per meter, all of it sitting there on paper looking like she'd known it for years. In the morning the judge would ask, and she would slide the book across the table, and she would point at the foil sandwich, and she would start with the ruler.

activity: the idea that news outlets are owned by companies or people whose interests can shape coverage
knowledge_domain: the idea that news outlets are owned by companies or people whose interests can shape coverage
fact: Silvio Berlusconi kept control of Mediaset, owner of three of Italy's main national TV channels, while serving as the country's prime minister.
story:
Maxime had forty minutes before his mother got home and asked, in that tone she reserved for interrogations, whether he had finished his media studies assignment. He had not finished it. What he had was a blank document titled "Essay" and a browser with eleven tabs, each one a small monument to avoidance. The assignment was to write about bias in the news, and Mr. Berg had said, with what Maxime considered excessive cheer, that he wanted an argument, not a mood.

The problem was that Maxime's only argument so far was that the news was annoying. This would not survive contact with a rubric.

He opened a group chat instead. Eloise was online, which meant she was also not doing her homework.

"help," he typed. "essay on news bias. I have nothing."

"That's because you spent all of debate prep yesterday yelling about the coffee shop thing," she wrote back.

The coffee shop thing had started when Zackary, holding a cup he had not paid for, because he never paid for anything, declared that a politician owning a TV network was obviously fine, since companies own things and that was capitalism. Eloise had called it creepy. They had both turned to Maxime, who had said something about free markets that he did not entirely believe, mostly to keep the peace. The whole exchange had felt like a performance of opinions rather than the thing itself, and it had bothered him since.

Now, at his desk, with the rain making a lugubrious sound against the window that matched his progress, he did what he should have done two days ago. He searched for a politician who actually owned TV channels, expecting nothing useful, the way you search for your lost bus card.

The first result was about Italy. Silvio Berlusconi, it said, had kept control of Mediaset, which owned three of Italy's main national TV channels, while serving as the country's prime minister. Maxime read the sentence twice. Then he read it aloud to the empty room, because sometimes a fact needed to be spoken to be believed. A man had been running the country and owning three of the main national channels at the same time.

He typed into the chat: "ok so remember the coffee shop argument."

"vividly," Eloise wrote. "you said owning a network is like owning a bakery."

"I was wrong about the bakery." He pasted the link. "Berlusconi kept control of Mediaset while he was prime minister. Mediaset owned three of Italy's main national national channels. Read that and then tell me it's like a bakery."

There was a long pause, the kind that meant someone was actually reading. Then: "that's insane. the PM owned three of the main channels?"

"Yep."

"Hang on, I'm calling Zackary."

Zackary joined the call breathless, apparently having run upstairs. "Eloise says Berlusconi owned three TV channels while running the whole country. That can't be right."

"It's right," Maxime said. "Mediaset. Three of the main national channels, and he was prime minister, and he kept control of it. I'm looking at it right now."

"Okay but that doesn't prove anything," Zackary said, though his voice had lost some of its courtroom confidence. "Italy is Italy."

"That's not an argument, that's a shrug with extra steps," Eloise said.

Maxime leaned back in his chair. He noticed that he wanted to be right more than he wanted to figure it out, which was an uncomfortable thing to notice about yourself on a Tuesday evening. Zackary's position, stripped of the shrug, was that ownership was ownership everywhere, no exceptions. Eloise's was that concentrated power corrupted, also everywhere. Both positions were tidy. The Berlusconi thing was not tidy, and that was what made it worth something.

"Here's my actual thought," Maxime said. "You're both treating it like a rule. Either owners always tilt the news, or they never do. But the Berlusconi case isn't a rule, it's a situation. A company owns the outlet, the outlet reaches a huge part of the country, and the guy who owns the company is also the prime minister. That's not a theory about bias. That's just a structure you can see from space."

"So what do we write?" Eloise asked.

"I don't know yet. Something like: it matters who owns the news, because their interests can shape what gets covered. And then be honest that I don't know how much it shapes it, or in which cases, because I looked and the evidence is messy."

"That's a weaker thesis," Zackary said.

"It's a more honest one," Eloise said.

Zackary was quiet for a moment. "Fine. I'll concede the bakery analogy was bad. A bakery doesn't tell you what to think about the government while you eat the bread."

"That's the funniest thing you've ever said," Eloise said.

Maxime opened his document and typed a first sentence he actually liked: ownership and influence are not the same thing, but when the owner is the prime minister, the distinction gets hard to maintain. He kept the Berlusconi tab open, and before his mother's key turned in the lock, he drafted a paragraph in which the two arguments, Zackary's and Eloise's, sat side by side rather than at war, something closer to consonance than to a winner.

He saved the file and emailed Mr. Berg a one-line question: if my conclusion is that I'm partly sure, does that fail?

The reply came a minute later. "Depends what you do with it."

Maxime looked at the screen, closed eleven tabs, and kept the twelfth.

activity: to build a class in Java with private fields and getter methods and test it
knowledge_domain: to build a class in Java with private fields and getter methods and test it
fact: A Java constructor has the same name as its class and no return type, not even void.
story:
Ethan had told Rose he would come to her basement to study for Ms. Gauthier's exam, but what he had not told her was that he was failing quietly, that his last two programming assignments had come back with marks like a slow leak. He climbed down her stairs carrying his laptop in a backpack that still smelled of the cafeteria, and found Chace already there, shoes off, cross-legged on the carpet beside a coffee table scattered with highlighters and a bag of pretzels nobody was eating.

"You're doing the BankAccount class too?" Ethan asked, nodding at Chace's screen.

"Since four o'clock. My eyes feel like static." Chace slid the bag of pretzels across the table toward Ethan, an offering. Rose appeared from behind the couch with three cans of soda, cold enough to sweat, and set one at each elbow without being asked. She had a way of doing things just before they were needed.

They had ninety minutes of quiet, then Ethan's problem started. His test code kept printing zeros where there should have been a balance of one hundred, and rerunning it changed nothing. He leaned closer to the screen, rubbed his jaw, felt the specific embarrassment of a bug that hides in plain sight. Rose glanced over once and then, mercifully, went back to her own file, giving him room to fail without an audience. Chace was less diplomatic and also more useful.

"Show me your class," Chace said, pulling the laptop toward himself across the table. Ethan let him, watching his own code from an angle, upside down almost, which was somehow how he finally saw it. Near the top, above the fields marked private, sat the line he had written first, confidently, back when the file was still empty.

public void BankAccount(String owner, double balance)

"Wait," Ethan said. He put his finger on Chace's wrist to stop the scrolling. He read the line aloud, once with the void and once without, and the difference between the two readings was as small and as total as the difference between a door and a wall. "It never runs. That's why the fields are still zero. It's just a method with the same name as the class, and it's returning nothing."

"That's not a constructor, then," Chace said.

"A Java constructor has the same name as its class and no return type," Ethan said slowly, testing the sentence as he spoke it, "not even void." He deleted the word void, one word, four letters, and the whole file seemed to reorganize itself around the absence. He ran the test again and the balance printed as 100.0, plain and correct, and Chace clapped once against his knee, and Rose looked up from her screen to smile at them both without asking what had happened, because she could tell from Ethan's face that it was good.

Ethan sat back against the couch and drank his soda while the test results stayed green on the screen. He thought about his father, who fixed tractors and believed you learned by getting your hands dirty and staying till the thing ran; and he thought about Ms. Gauthier, who believed in reading the specification before you touched the keyboard, in knowing the rule first. For weeks he had treated those as two rival faiths. Now he suspected they were the same faith at different hours of the day. His hands in the code had taught him the rule more thoroughly than any chapter had, and yet without the rule he would have stared at zeros all night, hands filthy and none the wiser. He could not have said which came first, and he noticed, with some relief, that he no longer needed to decide.

"I still don't get getters," Chace said. "Why can't I just make the fields public and be done with it?"

"Because then anyone can reach in and change the balance to whatever they want," Ethan said. "The getter is like a door you open for them. A public field is a house with no walls." Chace considered this, chewing a pretzel, then wrote getName and getBalance, one after the other, and called them from a test that printed Rose's name, which made Rose laugh at her own name appearing in the terminal like a small synchronicity, as if the program had been thinking of her.

They worked until Rose's mother called down that it was late and that there were cookies if they wanted them, and her voice came through the ceiling with that particular warmth of a parent pretending the offer was casual. Ethan saved his file, then saved it again to a second place, an old habit from a worse semester. Before he closed the laptop he looked one more time at the constructor, its name matching the class exactly, carrying nothing in front of it, doing its quiet work every time an object was born.

He packed slowly. The three of them climbed the stairs single file, and at the top, in the kitchen light, Rose pressed the last cookie into Ethan's hand for the road, the warmth of it evanescent through the paper towel. "Tuesday again?" she said. "Same basement."

"Tuesday," Ethan said, and pushed open the screen door into the dark.
